md: TTT here does not mean fine-tuning the LLM on your prompt. The network's ordinary parameters stay frozen at inference. Only the small per-layer weights $W$ change, they start from $W_0$ for every sequence, and they are discarded afterwards, just like an RNN's hidden state.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: One lock, many cores: why a shared slab cache stops scaling
md: A shared lock caps allocator throughput at $1/c$ no matter how many cores you add. The fix is not a faster lock but keeping the common path on state that only one CPU (or thread) touches, and going to shared state rarely and in batches.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Stacking: let the rare thing rise to the top
md: Rare is not malicious and common is not safe. PEAK: "Just because something is abnormal doesn't mean it's malicious." And an attacker who pushes the same tool to every machine at once (ransomware deployment through a management tool, a compromised software update) is not rare at all. Stacking finds the start of an intrusion well and its widespread final stage poorly.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Collection: where intelligence comes from, and what it is worth
md: Collect against requirements, prefer sources about you (internal telemetry, sector peers), and measure every external source by what it contributes: relevance, timeliness and unique hits, not volume. For a question like PIR-1, check CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue from *Security from zero* first.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Attribution: levels, evidence and its limits
md: Technical evidence shows *what* and often *where*: tools, infrastructure, keyboard layouts, working hours. It rarely shows *who pays*. Be wary of attribution that rests on one artefact, on a tool many groups use, or on a country's motive alone, and never copy another vendor's attribution into your report without its confidence and basis.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Ranking threats: risk, DREAD and why it fell out of favour
md: Ranking is a conversation, not a calculation. Use a simple scale, write down the reasons behind each rating, and make sure every threat ends with an explicit response: mitigate, eliminate, transfer or accept.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Promotion: finding hot pages trapped in slow memory
md: Promotion needs two signals: *is this page hot* (recency of access) and *can we afford to move it* (free space, rate limit). Missing either one turns tiering into a migration storm.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: What TLS promises, and what it does not
md: TLS gives you an encrypted, tamper-evident channel to **whoever holds the private key for a certificate naming that host**. Everything else (is that the right host, is the CA trustworthy, is the code bug-free) is a separate question.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: HSTS, preloading and why key pinning fell out of favour
md: Mobile apps still pin. If you pin, pin to more than one key (RFC 7469 itself required a backup pin), prefer pinning a CA or intermediate key you control over a leaf, have a way to ship new pins before old keys retire, and remember that pinning cannot help against bugs like goto fail, where the chain is genuine but the handshake signature is never checked.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Autotuning, num_warps, num_stages and when to use Triton
md: Triton moves the hard parts of a CUDA kernel (coalescing, shared memory, barriers, pipelining) into the compiler, and leaves you the decisions that need knowledge of the problem: the tiling, the program-to-tile order, the masks, and a short list of configs to autotune.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant
md: A unikernel is **one application plus only the OS code it uses, linked into one image that boots directly on a hypervisor**. The hypervisor, not a guest kernel, is the isolation boundary.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Paravirtual I/O up close: one packet through a virtqueue
md: A virtqueue is **three shared arrays and two counters**. Data moves through memory for free; only **notifications** cost VM exits and interrupts, so batching, suppression and polling set the price of each packet.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
md: Deleting from hnswlib with `markDelete` only sets a flag. The node keeps its edges and is still used for routing; it is just filtered out of results. Lots of deletions therefore still cost traversal time until the index is rebuilt.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Weight handoff: from 3D-HybridEngine to sleep, wake and streaming
md: Today's handoff in one line: sleep frees the rollout, the trainer updates, then weights come back first, stream in by bucket and are sliced by the inference engine's own loader, the trainer's memory leaves, and the KV cache comes back last. Across GPU pools the same stream goes over a checkpoint engine, optionally as a sparse delta.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: World models, and why Genie learns one from unlabelled video
md: A learned world model is not the real environment. Ha and Schmidhuber found their agent discovered an *adversarial policy* that exploited flaws in M, doing well in the dream but not in reality. They raised a sampling temperature, a knob that scales how random M's samples are (higher means more random), to make the dream noisier and harder to exploit. Every world model in this course shares this risk.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Hypervisor designs: where device models run and what one bug reaches
md: Ask two questions of any hypervisor: which host code does a guest reach directly, and what privileges does that code hold? The best designs put device models in small, unprivileged, per-VM sandboxes, so one bug buys one sandbox, not the host.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Attestation: proving what is running before you send it secrets
md: The most common attestation bug is not cryptographic: a verifier that checks the signature but not the nonce (replay), not the measurement (any VM passes), or not the debug policy (the host can decrypt). Check every field you depend on, and fail closed.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
md: Kumar et al. note fine-tuning can still beat linear probing out of distribution when the pretrained features are weak or the shift is small (CIFAR-10 to CIFAR-10.1, a fresh test set collected the same way as the original). LP-FT is a strong default, not a law.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Codebook collapse: measuring and fixing unused codes
md: Bigger codebooks do not automatically mean more capacity. FSQ, a quantizer with a fixed grid of codes that lesson 5 covers (Mentzer et al., 2023), found that VQ's reconstruction FID was best at about 2^11 codes and then stopped improving, at the same point where VQ's codebook usage began to drop, despite an entropy regulariser (an extra loss that rewards spreading choices evenly over the codes).

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Inside FLASH_ATTN's forward: from slot_mapping to one kernel call
md: vLLM deleted its original PagedAttention CUDA kernel (`paged_attention_v1`/`v2`) in July 2026 (PR #47361). Older posts that call it vLLM's attention kernel describe history. On main, every backend reads pages inside its own kernel through `block_table`. The *PagedAttention and prefix caching* course covers how that kernel worked.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: CUDA graphs: padding, support levels and mode downgrades
md: CUDA graphs constrain attention through shape (pad to a captured size), address (persistent metadata buffers) and kernel choice (`AttentionCGSupport`). The weakest backend in the model sets the graph mode for everyone.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Where VLMs fail and how they are evaluated
md: A high benchmark score does not mean the model looked at the image. The BlindTest paper cites prior work finding that 42.9% of MMMU questions can be answered without the image. Build a small eval from your own documents, with the image-free baseline as a control.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Making wait-free fast: fast path, slow path, and when to bother
md: Check every layer. A wait-free algorithm is only as wait-free as its primitives and helpers: a `fetch_or` that compiles to a CAS loop, an allocator that takes a lock, or a reclamation scheme that can block will each reintroduce unbounded waiting.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Web testing as work: pentests, disclosure programmes and bounties
md: A pentest buys coverage of an agreed scope; a bug bounty buys the first valid report of each root cause; a VDP buys reports without payment. In all three the written rules, published or signed before testing, are what make the work legal.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: File inclusion: when a path parameter chooses the code that runs
md: Path traversal reads a file; file inclusion runs it. The fix for both is the same idea: the user picks from a list the server owns, never a path.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Origins and sites: how the browser names who owns a page
md: Same-site is not same-origin. `login.example.com` and `blog.example.com` are same-site but cross-origin. A weak subdomain (an old blog, a marketing page run by a vendor) is "same-site" with your login page, and cookie rules and SameSite (lesson 5) treat it as a friend.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Site isolation: separate processes as a second wall
md: Site isolation is **defence in depth** for the browser itself. It does not change what web pages are allowed to do, so it will not stop XSS, CSRF or a bad CORS policy. It limits the damage when the browser's own enforcement fails.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: SMB file shares and EternalBlue: how WannaCry spread
md: Worms need two things: a reachable service and a bug in it. Patching removes the bug; turning off SMBv1 and blocking 445 removes the reachability. Do both, because you will never patch everything on time.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Public Wi-Fi and captive portals in the HTTPS era
md: On public Wi-Fi, TLS with correct certificate validation is what protects you, not the Wi-Fi layer. The risks that remain are the places where TLS is missing (first HTTP request, portal page) or broken (apps that skip validation).

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
md: Misconception: more workers always means more throughput. With one locked queue, past the knee extra workers only add waiters on the same lock and the same cache line. The model here is deliberately simple, but the cap of 1/c is real for any serial section.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Cheap scaling studies, continual training and failure modes
md: WSD is **not fully schedule-free**. Optimal peak LR still shifts with training length: Bergsma et al. (2025) quote Shen et al. puzzling that the best WSD LRs differ by token count, and Hägele et al. found the best cooldown peak LR was about half the best cosine peak. Tune the peak LR at roughly the length you care about; lesson 7 gives the evidence and a rule for adjusting it.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: MSG_ZEROCOPY: sending from your own memory safely
md: Writing into a buffer before its id completes does not crash anything, but it corrupts your own stream: the modified bytes may go out on the wire or in a retransmission. The kernel docs: kernel integrity is not affected, but a buggy program can corrupt its own data stream.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Evaluating zero-shot classifiers and choosing thresholds
md: Zero-shot replaces training data with design choices. Make those choices on a labeled dev set: compare templates or descriptions, pick argmax or per-label thresholds by the cost of errors, and re-check whenever the labels change.
